finding.claim: Unauthenticated POST /restore passes attacker-controlled bytes to Marshal.load, which can instantiate arbitrary Ruby objects and so allows remote code execution through gadget chains.
finding.source: app.rb:6 params[:state], any POST /restore request parameter (body or query). No authentication or origin check precedes it.
finding.sink: app.rb:6 Marshal.load(Base64.decode64(...)). Marshal's format can construct any loadable class and invoke its _load/marshal_load/initialize-style hooks during deserialization.

trace.note: post "/restore" route defined with no before-filter, auth, or signature check.
params[:state] read from the request, base64-decoded, and passed directly to Marshal.load.
Deserialized object is returned via state.inspect, so the attacker also sees a textual rendering of whatever objects were built (information disclosure aid for building payloads).

finding.guards_checked: None on the path: no authentication/authorization (no Sinatra filters in app.rb), no HMAC or signature over the state blob, no class allowlist, no size limit, no fallback to a data-only format (contrast with JSON on /import). Base64 is an encoding, not a control. Case 18 (unsafe deserializer on request content) is the matching pattern; no decoy applies. Preconditions: the service must be reachable by the attacker (bind address not set in file; Sinatra defaults to localhost only in development, so exposure depends on deployment). Full code execution requires a usable gadget chain among classes loaded in the process; a working chain was not verified. Even without RCE, the endpoint lets an unauthenticated caller construct arbitrary objects and read them back via inspect. Treat as critical if network-exposed. Fix: do not use Marshal for untrusted input; use a data-only format (JSON) with a schema, and authenticate the route.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.rb:5 declares `post "/restore"` with no before-filter, auth check, or signature/HMAC; app.rb:6 passes `params[:state]` through Base64.decode64 straight into Marshal.load with no class allowlist or size limit; app.rb:7 returns `state.inspect`. The only other file content is the `/import` route at app.rb:10-13, which uses JSON and is not a control on this path.
verdict.reason: The trace at app.rb:5-7 matches the code exactly, and an anonymous caller can send any `state` parameter to the unauthenticated route, so Marshal.load at app.rb:6 is reached with attacker bytes. Exploitation requires the service to be network-reachable (the bind address is not set in app.rb), and RCE through a gadget chain was not verified, so the "RCE" wording is stronger than what was shown, but the unsafe Marshal deserialization of untrusted input is real.
